To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

gay/bisexual substance abusers who use condoms during unprotected anal sex while under influence of alcohol and other drugs are more likely to have a college degree, more likely to have more than $20, 000 annual income, less likely to use amphetamine or cocaine, less likely to report a high frequency of anal sex, more likely to approve of having sex only with a partner who is in love, more likely to perceive safer sex as community norm and more likely to have encouragement to practice safer sex

men who use condoms when they drink and/or use drugs are more likely than those who do not use condoms to have a college education, to have a higher income, to use fewer drugs, to approve of sex with love, to believe safer sex is the norm, and to have encouragement to practice safer sex.

gay men who use alcohol and/or other substances and have unprotected anal sex while under their influence are less likely to approve sex without love and to have encouragement from their friends to practice safer-sex than those who use substances but always practice safer sex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of alcohol/drug use and sexual behavior on HIV transmission.
understanding the relationship between substance use and sexual behavior in the gay/bisexual community.
the influence of alcohol/drug use on sexual behavior and the role of social and cognitive variables in the relationship between alcohol/drug use and sexual behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the men who use condoms while under the influence are more likely to be college educated, have a higher income, use amyl nitrate and cocaine less frequently, have more sex while under the influences of alcohol and drugs, have a higher approval of sex without love, have a lower perception that safer sex is community norm, and have less encouragement from friends to use condoms.

men who are more likely to have unprotected anal sex while under influence of alcohol and other drugs tend to have less education, have a lower income, use amyl nitrate and cocaine, have more anal sex, and have less positive attitudes toward safer sex.

men who have consistently unprotected anal sex while under influence of alcohol and drugs are significantly less likely to have a college degree, have less income, use cocaine and amyl nitrite, report more frequency of anal sex, approve of sex without affection, and have less encouragement from friends to use safer sex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two groups of men differed significantly on a wide variety of variables.
men who use condoms while under the influence are more likely to have safer sex in general.

men whose anal sex under the influence of drugs is consistently unprotected are more likely to have less than a college level education and less income, to use amyl and cocaine more frequently, and to have more unprotected anal sex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not enough to simply tell gay/bisexual drug and/or alcohol users to use condoms.
there are many different factors that contribute to sexual risk-taking.
it is important to look beyond HIV status and to examine a variety of factors that may influence sexual safety.
